newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Money data should give S.African bonds fresh boost.
newsitem.headline: Money data should give S.African bonds fresh boost.

text.p: Better-than-expected December money supply and credit extension figures should give South African bonds a fresh boost, and could even bring forward a hoped for interest rate cut, economists said on Tuesday.
"It's very good data -- bonds will probably go to 15.25 (percent) tommorrow," said Nick Barnardt, economist at BOE NatWest.
The benchmark R150 government stock was last yielding 15.41 percent in after hours trade, down from 15.435 ahead of release of the figures at 1500 GMT.
The Reserve Bank said year-on-year M3 money supply grew 13.73 percent in December from a revised 15.18 percent in November, while annual private sector credit growth was 15.75 percent.
A Reuters consensus poll of economist forecast M3 growth of 14.3 percent while private credit was seen expanding 16.3 percent.

Analysts said the growth rates had been deflated by very high year-ago comparative figures, but the picture was still encouraging for the two monetary aggregates which are closely monitored by Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals.
"It should be positive for the bond market, although for technical reasons we might see some resistance around current levels," said Equisec economist Dawie Roodt.
"We should see the figures down again in January and that means we might see a Bank rate cut by March."

The general consensus among economists has been that Stals will hold his hand on the Bank rate -- currently 17 percent -- until mid-year. Stals reiterated again last week that he remained concerned about excessive money supply and credit growth.
The 1996 guideline for M3 growth is six to 10 percent. The Bank has yet to set 1997 guidelines.
The good money supply figures come hard on the heels of better-than-expected inflation data for December released earlier on Tuesday.

Consumer price inflation rose to its highest level since June 1995 last month at 9.4 percent, from 9.2 percent in November, but this was better than the forecast 9.6 percent. Analysts also noted the increase was largely due to one-off housing and transport costs.
At the same time an improving inflow of capital has nudged down South Africa's money market shortage to below 9.9 billion rand, leading to a steady reduction in short-term interest rates.
The 90-day BA rate was slightly lower at between 16.40 to 16.60 percent on Tuesday from 16.45 to 16.60 on Monday while three-month NCD rates were steady at between 17.10 and 17.25 percent.
